ta-l1d1q4-d1e3498.summary: Transitional paragraph introducing the third inquiry of Distinction 1, on those who enjoy and those who use. It treats first those who enjoy, then those who use.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3510.summary: First objection, arguing that insensible creatures enjoy. Enjoyment is desire brought to rest in its end. Every creature, even an insensible one, naturally desires its end and can attain it and rest in it.
claims: Every creature, even insensible, naturally desires and can rest in its end.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3513.summary: Second objection, arguing that brute animals enjoy. Enjoyment concerns what is sought for itself and not referred to another. Brutes seek things in which they delight without referring them to anything further, since they lack ordering reason.
claims: Brutes delight in things without referring them to anything further.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3516.summary: Third objection. By natural love one can love God above all things, since he is naturally known to be the highest good and so lovable for his own sake. So a human being with natural endowments alone (in naturalibus tantum) can enjoy God.
claims: By natural love one can love God above all things as the highest good.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3520.summary: Fourth objection. Someone in mortal sin may set God as the ultimate end of some action without referring it to anything else, which is enjoyment. So even a sinner can enjoy God.
claims: A sinner may make God the ultimate end of a particular action.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3523.summary: A contrary objection, that even the just do not enjoy God in this life. Enjoyment is the delighted will's rest in what is known for its own sake, and as long as one is a wayfarer one does not rest.
claims: The wayfarer's will does not yet rest.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3526.summary: Objection that even the blessed do not enjoy. According to Lombard's text, whoever enjoys something needs it, and whoever needs something lacks it. The blessed do not lack God, so they do not enjoy him.
claims: Whatever enjoys something needs it, and what needs something lacks it.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3529.summary: A corollary of the preceding objection: God does not enjoy himself either, since he does not need himself.
claims: God does not need himself.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3532.summary: Thomas's determination. Enjoyment implies delight in the end, and delight exists only in a knower (Plato: delight is a perceived generation into what suits one's nature). So insensible creatures, which do not know, neither delight nor enjoy. Enjoyment properly concerns only the ultimate end, which brutes neither apprehend nor can order proximate ends toward, lacking reason, so they do not properly enjoy. A sinner places their ultimate end where it is not and, having no true end, does not truly enjoy. Since perfect enjoyment requires perfect delight, which is impossible before the end is attained, the just do not enjoy perfectly in this life; only the blessed, who have attained the end, enjoy truly, perfectly, and properly.
claims: Enjoyment requires knowledge, since delight exists only in a knower.
Brutes and sinners do not properly or truly enjoy, because they do not apprehend or possess the true ultimate end.
The just in this life enjoy imperfectly; only the blessed enjoy perfectly.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3535.summary: Reply to the first objection. All desire follows on knowledge, but the desire of insensible creatures follows not a knowledge within them but that of the first mover, whoever it is, who orders each thing to its end. Without knowledge of their own, they have neither delight nor enjoyment.
claims: Natural appetite in insensible things follows the knowledge of the mover who orders them to their end, not knowledge of their own.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3539.summary: Reply to the second objection. Animals delight in an end, but that end is not ultimate. It is referred to something further, not by them but by the first orderer who orders all things to himself. Since they delight only in the ultimate end they apprehend, not in the ultimate end simply, they are said to enjoy only improperly.
claims: Animals enjoy only improperly, delighting in an end that is ultimate for their apprehension but not simply ultimate.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3542.summary: Reply to the third objection. Delight follows perfect operation, and an operation is perfect when it proceeds from a habit. Acquired or natural habits do not sufficiently and proximately perfect us for heavenly beatitude. Augustine says the beloved creature is present to the lover by a familiar contact for experiencing its sweetness, but delight in the Creator is of a quite different kind. Without a gratuitous habit, then, there is no delight sufficient for enjoyment. Alternatively, natural love implies only a natural inclination, not an operation in act, and that inclination is actualized through the habit of charity.
claims: Without a gratuitous habit there is no delight sufficient for enjoyment of God.
Natural love of God is an inclination brought into act through charity.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3548.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. Someone in mortal sin habitually loves something above God, even if not always actually. So they do not enjoy God but enjoy that to which they order everything.
claims: One in mortal sin habitually loves something above God and so enjoys that, not God.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3551.summary: Reply to the fifth objection, distinguishing two kinds of rest. Rest of desire occurs when desire stops at something for whose sake it does and seeks everything and desires nothing further; in this way the just person's will rests in God in this life. Rest of motion occurs when the sought terminus is reached, and this will be in heaven. Rest of motion makes for perfect enjoyment, rest of desire for imperfect enjoyment.
claims: The wayfarer's will has rest of desire in God, yielding imperfect enjoyment; rest of motion, yielding perfect enjoyment, belongs to heaven.
concepts: rest of desire vs. rest of motion

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3554.summary: Reply to the sixth objection, distinguishing two senses of needing something. In one sense one needs what one depends on for existence. In this sense all things need God, since, as Gregory says, all would tend to nothing unless the Creator's hand held them, for God is the cause not only of things' becoming but of their being. In this sense the blessed need God. In another sense one needs what one does not yet have, and in this sense they do not.
claims: All creatures, including the blessed, need God as the cause sustaining their being.
God is the cause not only of the becoming of things but of their being.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3557.summary: Reply to the last objection. The principle that one who enjoys needs what is enjoyed holds only when the two differ in essence, which is not the case in divine enjoyment. God therefore enjoys himself perfectly. Gregory says he is glorious who, enjoying himself, needs no added praise.
claims: God enjoys himself perfectly, since in him the one enjoying and the one enjoyed are not distinct in essence.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3575.summary: First objection, that no one will use anything in heaven. A road is unnecessary once the end is reached; Bernard asks what need of a ladder one has who already holds the throne. Use concerns means to the end, which are like a road, so the blessed will have no use.
claims: Means to an end are like a road, unnecessary once the end is attained.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3584.summary: Second objection. To use is to refer one thing to another, which requires thinking one thing after another. According to Augustine there are no shifting thoughts (cogitationes volubiles) in heaven, so there will be no use there.
claims: Referring one thing to another requires successive thought.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3587.summary: Sed contra. Love of God and neighbour remains in heaven, since charity never fails (1 Cor. 13:8). The neighbour will never be loved for their own sake but for God's, so the love of use will always remain there.
claims: Love of neighbour, which remains in heaven, is always for the sake of God and thus a form of use.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3599.summary: Thomas's determination. Use concerns means to the end, which are of two kinds. Some include and touch the end and do not conflict with its perfection, as the dispositions of matter remain with the substantial form: natural perfections, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and whatever does not imply imperfection in its concept. These will be used in heaven. Others stand at a distance from the end, like motion, and are incompatible with it because of their imperfection: punishments, acts of faith and hope, food, and the like. These will not be used in heaven.
claims: Means that include the end and imply no imperfection, such as natural perfections and the gifts of the Spirit, will be used in heaven.
Means that are distant from the end, such as faith, hope, punishments, and food, will cease.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3602.summary: Reply to the first objection, by analogy with knowledge and nature. One comes to know principles through what follows from them, but once one has them one knows them better and no longer needs the consequences to know them, while the knowledge of the consequences is not lost but perfected through the principles. In the same way a human comes to God through creatures. Once God is possessed, they no longer need creatures to have him, and through him they come to the perfect use of everything else. Likewise in nature, form is acquired through dispositions but, once possessed, is the principle of all accidents.
claims: Once God is attained, creatures are no longer needed as a way to him but are used more perfectly through him.
Knowledge of consequences is perfected, not lost, when principles are possessed.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3605.summary: Reply to the second objection. 'Shifting thought' properly means discursive reasoning, which does not immediately see what it seeks and must proceed from one thing to another. In heaven, whatever is sought will appear at once and without difficulty in the divine light, and humans will understand with a deiform intellect, like the angels. Succession of thoughts is not excluded in heaven, however, and still less the ordering of one thing to another, which can exist even without succession.
claims: In heaven discursive reasoning is replaced by immediate understanding in the divine light.
Ordering one thing to another can exist without temporal succession, so use remains in heaven.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3608.summary: Concedes the sed contra argument that use remains in heaven through love of neighbour.

ta-l1d1q4-d1e3619.summary: The expositio textus raises and resolves a series of difficulties in Lombard's wording in Distinction 1. (1) The division into things and signs is a division by opposed concepts (absolute and relative), not by opposed things, so one thing can be both a sign and a thing, and 'thing' is taken broadly or strictly. Creatures signify God only secondarily, since they were not instituted for that purpose. (2) Treating things before signs suits teaching, which must present things first because signs are taken from their likeness to things, whereas learning proceeds from signs to things. (3) Humans are 'between' the enjoyable and the usable. Ranked by rectitude of life, virtues are the greatest goods and natural powers middle goods; ranked by progress to beatitude, what beatifies is greatest, what participates in beatitude is middle, and what disposes to it is least. (4) The threefold division of things is not redundant: users progress toward the end, whereas usable things are a way to it. (5) Augustine's definition of 'use' is well formed, since 'what has come into use' is a circumlocution for the usable, the act's object. (6) No name fits God's excellence: we name things as we know them, from creatures, and abstract names signify the non-subsistent while concrete names signify the composite. (7) Hope delays and afflicts as concerning the absent, yet delights as making its object somehow present. (8) Multiple definitions of enjoyment and use are legitimate, since definitions can be given through different causes and properties. Thomas assigns each Augustinian definition its basis: object and habit, power, or a consequent property such as joy in what is possessed. (9) God's use of us differs from ours: he refers his use to our benefit and to his own goodness, as shown in works of mercy, creation, and justice. Evil, as privation, diminishes being. (10) 'Because he is good, we are' holds because, although creaturely perfections are exemplarily caused by distinct attributes, goodness has the character of end, the cause of causes. (11) Good and being differ in concept but are convertible in their supposits.
claims: The division of res and signum is by opposed concepts, not opposed things.
In teaching, things must be treated before signs, since signs are taken from their likeness to things.
Multiple definitions of one thing are legitimate when taken through different causes or properties.
Human names fall short of God, since abstract names signify the non-subsistent and concrete names the composite.
God uses creatures for their benefit and for his own goodness; evil as privation diminishes being.
Good and being are convertible in supposits while differing in concept.

ta-l1d1q4-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Question 4 announces the inquiry into those who enjoy and those who use, completing the threefold plan of Distinction 1.

ta-l1d1q4-Dd1e3502.summary: Article 1 asks who enjoys. Objections claim enjoyment for insensible creatures (natural desire for their end), brutes (delight without further reference), humans with natural endowments alone (natural love of God above all), and sinners (who may make God the end of an act). Others deny it to the just in this life (who do not yet rest), to the blessed (who do not lack God), and to God himself (who does not need himself). Thomas holds that enjoyment requires knowledge, since delight exists only in a knower, and concerns the true ultimate end. Insensible creatures and brutes therefore do not properly enjoy, and sinners do not truly enjoy. The just enjoy imperfectly, by rest of desire, and the blessed perfectly, by rest of motion. The replies trace natural appetite to the knowledge of the first orderer and require a gratuitous habit for delight sufficient for enjoyment. They distinguish needing God for one's being from lacking him, and affirm that God enjoys himself perfectly.
claims: Only rational knowers who possess the true ultimate end properly enjoy: the blessed perfectly, the just imperfectly.
Enjoyment of God requires a gratuitous habit, charity.
God enjoys himself perfectly.
concepts: rest of desire and of motion

ta-l1d1q4-Dd1e3567.summary: Article 2 asks whether anyone will use anything in heaven. Objections argue that the road is unnecessary once the end is reached, and that use requires the successive thought absent in heaven. The sed contra notes that love of neighbour, always for God's sake, remains. Thomas distinguishes means that include the end and imply no imperfection, which remain and will be used (natural perfections, the gifts of the Spirit), from means distant from the end, which cease (faith, hope, punishments, food). The replies compare the soul's ascent through creatures to knowledge of principles through their consequences: once God is possessed, creatures are used more perfectly through him. Discursive reasoning gives way to immediate understanding in the divine light without excluding ordered thought.
claims: Use remains in heaven for means that include the end and imply no imperfection.
Once God is possessed, creatures are used more perfectly through him.

ta-l1d1q4-Dd1e3612.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 1 resolves literal difficulties in Lombard's text. It covers the things/signs division as a division by concepts; the order of teaching things before signs; the ranking of goods; the sufficiency of the threefold division of things; Augustine's definitions of use and enjoyment, which are justified by different causes and properties; the inadequacy of human names for God; hope as both afflicting and delighting; and the asymmetry between God's use of creatures and ours. It ends with the attribution of being to divine goodness as final cause and with the convertibility of good and being.
claims: The res/signum division is by concepts, not by things.
Multiple definitions of use and enjoyment are justified by different causes and properties.
God uses creatures for their benefit and his own goodness; good and being are convertible.

ta-l1d1q4.summary: Quaestio 4 of Book I, Distinction 1 completes the distinction's inquiry by asking about the subjects of enjoyment and use, and closes with an exposition of the text. Article 1 limits enjoyment in the proper sense to rational knowers possessing the true ultimate end. It excludes insensible creatures, brutes, and sinners, grants imperfect enjoyment to the just in this life and perfect enjoyment to the blessed, and affirms God's perfect self-enjoyment. Article 2 holds that use continues in heaven for means that imply no imperfection, as creatures come to be used more perfectly through God once he is possessed. The Expositio clarifies Lombard's conceptual vocabulary. It covers things and signs, the definitions of uti and frui, the limits of divine naming, and goodness as the final cause of creaturely being.
claims: Only the blessed enjoy perfectly; the just enjoy imperfectly; brutes, insensible creatures, and sinners do not properly enjoy.
Use persists in heaven for means that include the end.
Lombard's division of things and signs and the Augustinian definitions of use and enjoyment are justified as divisions and definitions by concept and cause.
